subject: I'm lost and I need help!

messages.author: 09d404b8fd4515fa
messages.subject: I'm lost and I need help!
parts:
Hi, everyone,

            I’ve been volunteering with USFWS to conduct shrub-steppe songbird point counts for the past few years. This year, I made the mistake of volunteering to try and analyze the data for them, as they are understaffed and underpayed.  DISTANCE was the recommened tool.  I may have bitten off more than I can chew, but I’m trying to figure this out.  But I can’t get the data I have to match what Distance is asking for….I’m a birder, not a biologist or statistician. 

So, to summarize: in order to monitor shrub-steppe songbirds, avian point counts have been performed on the Fitzner-Eberhard Arid Lands Ecology Reserve (ALE), now part of the Hanford Reach National Monument according to the same protocol since 1997.  The only analysis performed to date analyzed data from 1997-2007 using repeated-measures mixed-effects models (Earnst et al 2009).  33 points were each sampled once per year, between May 1 and May 31.  The data collected records each bird sighted, and assigns it to a distance class of <50m, >50m, or as a “flyover”.  I would like to re-examine this data using the distance data to get a population density estimate for each species of concern for each year.  I would then attempt to correlate this to precipitation over previous winter, and to wildfire occurrence.

            So what I want is a number for D-hat for each species of interest for each year.  A quick glance over the data suggest that a given year results in about 500 sightings of about 30 species; half of the species are generally represented by a single individual, so I’ll ignore those.

            Bibby and Burgess (2000) suggests that getting the estimates I want using distance classes of 0 to 50m and 50m to infinity is possible, but I’m forced to assume a half-normal model for the detection curve.  That’s okay.  But what I don’t get is how to match up the data I have in hand to Distance 6.2’s data hierarchy.  “Observation,” obviously, is each individual sighting of a bird, with the distance.  “Sample” is going to be the individual point.  But where I’m stuck is defining the “Stratum” and “Global” layers.  Do I need to do each year as separate project?  Do I need to break it down to one species in one year equals one project?  If I do that, can I just get rid of the “stratum” layer?

            Other factors that could apply once I have this figured out is the time of day each sample was made, and also, observations are classified by time since the count started (0-3min, 3-5min, 5-10min) this means that I could start truncating the data, to get  a range for D-hat, as more time means more observations made.  But that can wait until I have a better understanding of the program.

            So for now, can anyone point me to what I need to do to get the data into Distance to get a basic density per species per year?  I realize that I’m asking a lot, but even some examples of similar projects or specific references to the User’s Guide or anything would be a help.  I’m trying to work it out, but I feel stuck.  I watched several YouTube videos by Eric Rexstad, but I’m still lost.  Thanks for anything you folks can provide.

 

Chad,  from Richland, WA, USA

References:

Bibby, C. and Burgess, N.  2000.  Bird Census Tecchniques, Second Edition.  Academic Press.

Earnst, S. L., Newsome, H. L., Laframboise, W. L., & Laframboise, N. (2009). Avian response to wildfire in interior columbia basin shrubsteppe. The Condor, 111(2), 370-376. doi:http://dx.doi.org/10.1525/cond.2009.080109

messages.author: f2122b34f1aa6e95
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] I'm lost and I need help!
parts:
Chad

Congratulations for volunteering your services.  Your question has quite a few facets a) data structure, b) detection function models and c) "other factors".

Regarding the mechanical aspects of getting your data into a format that Distance can analyse, I suggest you have a look at the sample projects that ship with the software.  There are three projects that you should examine (in increasing order of relevance):
 - amakihi.  Hawaii songbird study with 41 stations and 7 seasonal visits; there were 3 covariates considered in modelling the detection function.
 - housewren.  This has 10 plots, each with multiple points.  The points have multiple visits with data collected by multiple observers.  It is a songbird riparian habitat survey in Colorado, described in Section 8.6 of Buckland et al. (2001).
 - "songbird"  This was a study of multiple species in 4 pastures over 2 years (pasture x year considered strata).  This study is described in Section 8.7 of Buckland et al. (2001).

Examining these projects you will see the "global" layer is the study area, with "region" constituting strata for which you wish to have estimates.  In your situation, you might consider years as strata, similar to the "songbird" project.

Regarding your second point, regarding fitting detection functions to these data, you are correct that you might be able to fit a half-normal detection function (without adjustments) to the data collected according to the protocol you describe.  However there are two challenges to this.  First, animal movement causes bias in density estimates, particularly for point counts where observers are stationary; that suggests the "flyover" category should be excluded from your analysis.  Second, having but two distance categories considerably limits your modelling abilities.  Without exact distance measurements to the detections, you cannot use such things as Kolomogorov-Smirnov goodness of fit tests (described in Burnham et al. (2004), Chapter 11 of Advanced Distance Sampling, and available in Distance).  Instead you are left with chi-square goodness of fit tests, described in Section 3.4.4 of Buckland et al (2001).  With 2 distance categories, there are no degrees of freedom with which to assess the fit of your 1-parameter half-normal model (2 categories - 1 model parameter - 1 = 0 df for goodness of fit test).  That is a challenge, because you are left to make inference from a model, whose fit cannot be numerically assessed.

Your last point about other information to incorporate into modelling, as you say, can wait until you grapple with items a) and b).
